plan: Final batch to reach the verbal stop point: the S018-04 resubmission with its framing fixed, a words-in-context item whose trap is a literally true word, a central-idea item, a partial-disagreement cross-text item, a snow-insulation inference, a percent-versus-raw data item, subject-verb punctuation, a plural possessive, a contrast transition and a subject-introduction synthesis.

passages.title: The fast year
passages.text: In a poem, the speaker expresses surprise at how quickly the seasons pass.

passages.title: Ordered clashes
passages.text: Although the composer's early critics dismissed her harmonies as merely ______, later scholars showed that every apparent clash in her music followed strict rules she had worked out in her notebooks.

passages.title: Dating with lichens
passages.text: When a rockslide exposes fresh stone, lichens soon begin to colonize the bare surfaces. Some lichens grow at a slow and fairly steady rate, often only a fraction of a millimeter per year. By measuring the largest lichens on boulders from an undated rockslide and comparing them with lichens on surfaces of known age, such as dated gravestones, geologists can estimate roughly when the slide occurred.

passages.title: A town's decline (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
A historian argues that the plague of 1349 caused the decline of the market town of Hollin, which lost much of its population and trade in the years that followed.

Text 2
Tax records from Hollin show that the number of households paying the market tax fell steadily from about 1310 onward, as trade shifted to a new port downriver. The plague then sharply reduced a population that was already shrinking.

passages.title: Beetles under snow
passages.text: The larvae of a certain beetle spend the winter in the soil and die if the soil temperature falls below about −5°C. In one mountain valley, researchers found that larval survival dropped sharply during a winter with unusually little snow, even though average air temperatures that winter were milder than usual. This finding suggests that ______

passages.title: Ferry fares
passages.text:
After a ferry company cut its fares, it compared average daily ridership before and after the cut.
Season | Riders before cut | Riders after cut
Summer | 4,000 | 4,400
Winter | 1,000 | 1,300
A company analyst claims that, in percentage terms, the fare cut increased ridership more in winter than in summer.

passages.title: Water tower
passages.text: The engineer who designed the town's first water tower ______ the structure would last a century; it was finally replaced in 2019, 104 years after it was built.

passages.title: The Ferrer sisters
passages.text: Born a year apart, the painters Ana and Lucía Ferrer worked side by side for four decades. The ______ shared studio, a converted bakery in Valencia, is now a small museum.

passages.title: Telegraph ears
passages.text: Early telegraph operators were trained to transcribe incoming messages one letter at a time. Experienced operators, ______ often recognized whole words by the rhythm of their clicks and wrote them down before the final letters had even arrived.

passages.title: Fog nets
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Fog harvesting is a technique for collecting water from fog.
• Fine-mesh nets are stretched across the path of fog blowing in from the sea.
• Water droplets collect on the mesh and drip into troughs below.
• Villages in parts of Chile's Atacama Desert have used fog harvesting to obtain drinking water.

candidates.stem: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: "I walk to the river each morning / and count the herons standing in the reeds."
choices.B: "Snow lies on the field in winter / as it has lain there every year."
choices.C: "The maple I planted in April / is scarlet already, and stripped by the frost."
choices.D: "The summer was long and slow, / and the afternoons stretched into evening."

candidates.explanation: A tree planted in spring is already autumn-red and stripped by frost: the word "already" conveys surprise at the speed.

A.rationale: This describes a routine, not the speed of seasonal change.

B.rationale: This stresses sameness, not surprising speed.

D.rationale: This describes a season passing slowly, the opposite of the claim.

hints: Which quotation shows time moving fast?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate quotations about routine or slowness.

candidates.remember: Match the quotation to the specific feeling in the claim.
candidates.revision_note: S018-04 resubmitted relabelled easy (both solvers about 79%), with the framing rewritten as a claim about the poem because both solvers noted that 'The following text is adapted from a poem' promised a text that was not shown.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: every apparent clash in her music followed strict rules she had worked out
candidates.explanation: "Although" sets the critics' charge against the scholars' finding. The finding is that the clashes followed strict rules, so the charge it answers is that they were random: "haphazard."

B.rationale: Her harmonies do clash, and the scholars do not deny it; what they disprove is that the clashes were random.

C.rationale: Harmonies full of clashes would not be dismissed as ordinary or traditional.

D.rationale: Nothing in the text concerns sameness or repetition; the scholars' finding answers a charge of randomness.

hints: What did the later scholars prove about the clashes?

strategy.explanation: Predict the opposite of "followed strict rules."

candidates.remember: With "although," the blank is what the second half refutes.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Lichens are among the first organisms to grow on stone exposed by a rockslide.
choices.B: Lichens on gravestones grow more slowly than lichens on boulders from rockslides.
choices.C: Geologists can determine the exact year of any rockslide by examining its lichens.
choices.D: Slow, steady lichen growth lets geologists estimate when a rock surface was exposed.

candidates.evidence: geologists can estimate roughly when the slide occurred
candidates.explanation: The text explains that slow, steady lichen growth lets geologists estimate a slide's date. D states that idea; A is only a detail, and B and C go beyond the text.

A.rationale: This is a supporting detail; the text's point is how lichens are used for dating.

B.rationale: The text never compares growth rates on the two surfaces; gravestones simply supply known ages.

C.rationale: The text says "estimate roughly," not the exact year of any slide.

hints: What is the whole text building toward?

strategy.explanation: Look for the choice that covers the whole text, not one sentence.

candidates.remember: A main idea covers the whole text without overstating it.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the historian's claim in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the plague was the main cause of Hollin's decline
choices.B: By arguing that the plague sped up a decline that had already begun for other reasons
choices.C: By denying that the plague had any effect on Hollin's population
choices.D: By questioning whether tax records can show how many people lived in Hollin

candidates.evidence: The plague then sharply reduced a population that was already shrinking.
candidates.explanation: Text 2 dates the decline to about 1310 and the shift of trade downriver, but grants that the plague worsened it. The author would say the plague accelerated an existing decline, not that it caused it.

A.rationale: Text 2 shows the decline began decades before 1349, so the plague was not its starting cause.

C.rationale: Text 2 says the plague "sharply reduced" the population.

D.rationale: Text 2 relies on the tax records rather than doubting them.

hints: When did Hollin's decline begin, according to Text 2?

strategy.explanation: Find what Text 2 says about both the earlier trend and the plague.

candidates.remember: A partial disagreement is often the answer in cross-text items: check what the second text grants.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: milder air temperatures are themselves harmful to the larvae.
choices.B: the larvae can survive soil temperatures well below −5°C in most winters.
choices.C: a thick layer of snow normally keeps the soil warmer than the air above it.
choices.D: the larvae in the valley were killed by a cause unrelated to temperature.

candidates.evidence: even though average air temperatures that winter were milder than usual
candidates.explanation: Larvae die when the soil gets too cold. They died more in a mild winter that lacked snow, so the missing snow must normally protect the soil from cold: snow insulates the soil.

A.rationale: Nothing suggests warmth harms the larvae; the danger named is soil that is too cold.

B.rationale: The text states that the larvae die below about −5°C.

D.rationale: The text gives cold soil as the cause of death, and the snow explanation fits the evidence without inventing another cause.

hints: What was different about the winter when the larvae died?

strategy.explanation: Rule out choices that contradict the stated cause of death.

candidates.remember: When an outcome defies the obvious cause, look for the variable that changed.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the analyst's claim?

choices.A: Winter ridership rose by 30 percent after the cut, while summer ridership rose by 10 percent.
choices.B: Summer ridership rose by 400 riders after the cut, more than winter ridership rose.
choices.C: After the cut, summer ridership was more than three times winter ridership.
choices.D: Before the cut, average daily ridership in winter was 1,000.

candidates.evidence: in percentage terms, the fare cut increased ridership more in winter than in summer
candidates.explanation: Winter rose 300 on a base of 1,000 (30%); summer rose 400 on a base of 4,000 (10%). Only A gives the percentage comparison the claim needs.

B.rationale: This compares raw numbers, not percentages, and it favors summer, the opposite of the claim.

C.rationale: This compares the seasons with each other, not the size of each season's increase.

D.rationale: A single figure cannot show how much ridership changed.

hints: Does the claim compare raw increases or percentage increases?

strategy.explanation: Note the claim's exact measure before checking the table.

candidates.remember: Match the evidence to the claim's measure: percent change is not raw change.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: The engineer who designed the town's first water tower
candidates.explanation: The subject ("The engineer who designed the town's first water tower") leads straight into the verb and its object clause with no punctuation: "predicted that."

A.rationale: No comma belongs between a verb and the clause that is its object.

B.rationale: A comma here would separate the subject from its verb.

C.rationale: A colon must follow a complete independent clause; "The engineer ... predicted" is not complete without its object.

hints: Is the clause before the blank a complete sentence?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate punctuation that splits subject, verb and object.

candidates.remember: Never separate a subject from its verb, or a verb from its object, with punctuation.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: the painters Ana and Lucía Ferrer worked side by side
candidates.explanation: The studio belonged to both sisters, so the plural possessive "sisters'" is needed.

A.rationale: "Sister's" refers to one sister; the studio belonged to both.

C.rationale: The plural without an apostrophe does not show possession.

D.rationale: A plural ending in -s takes only an apostrophe.

hints: How many sisters owned the studio?

strategy.explanation: Decide singular or plural, then possessive or not.

candidates.remember: Plural possessive of a word ending in -s: add only an apostrophe.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: trained to transcribe incoming messages one letter at a time
candidates.explanation: Operators were trained to work letter by letter, but experienced ones recognized whole words: a contrast, so "however."

A.rationale: Recognizing whole words is not a result of being trained letter by letter; it departs from that training.

B.rationale: The second sentence does not illustrate letter-by-letter transcription; it describes a different practice.

C.rationale: The second sentence does not restate the first; it describes something different.

hints: Does the second sentence agree with the training or depart from it?
candidates.remember: Name the relationship between the sentences before choosing.

candidates.stem: The student wants to introduce fog harvesting to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Fog harvesting, in which fine-mesh nets catch droplets from fog, supplies drinking water to some Atacama villages.
choices.B: Villages in parts of Chile's Atacama Desert have obtained drinking water by using fog harvesting.
choices.C: Water droplets collect on fine-mesh nets stretched across the fog and drip into troughs below.
choices.D: Fog harvesting has been used in Chile, a country whose territory includes the Atacama Desert.

candidates.evidence: Fine-mesh nets are stretched across the path of fog
candidates.explanation: An audience unfamiliar with fog harvesting needs to learn what it is. Only A names the technique, explains how it works and gives an example of its use.

B.rationale: This names the technique but never explains what it is.

C.rationale: This describes part of the process without naming fog harvesting or saying what it is for.

D.rationale: This neither explains the technique nor says what it provides.

hints: What does an unfamiliar audience need first?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice for a definition of the technique.

candidates.remember: Introducing a subject means naming it and explaining what it is.
